method: three behavioural paradigms with three captive tammar wallabies trained to choose between coloured and white or grey stimuli on a computer-controlled LCD or monochromatic-light display: colour-mixing confusion points (Experiment 1), minimum wavelength difference (Experiment 2) and neutral-point test (Experiment 3)
conditions: three young adult wallabies (two males, one female) took part in the study but only one male (Miller) was used for Experiment 3; Experiment 3 monochromatic stimuli were intensity-matched to the white light assuming a 540 nm pigment and shown at 50, 75, 100, 150 and 200% of the white (450 nm matched only, 460 nm at 75 to 150% only), and choice did not change systematically with brightness; Experiment 2 stimuli were matched on M-cone intensity at 40% Michelson contrast with brightness varied by 40% and non-reinforced control trials about once every 20 trials; neutral point 484-487 nm by relative discrimination and 480-483 nm by absolute discrimination (the paper's range statement for the absolute series is 'appears to lie between 480 nm-483 nm'); in Experiment 3 choices for 480-487 nm were at chance (39.3-57.6% correct, P>0.29, binomial test against 50%); minimum wavelength discrimination was limited to roughly 440-500 nm, best near 460-480 nm and about 4 nm at best; the animals preferred relative discrimination and learned absolute discrimination only after a relative-discrimination stage (absolute training without prior relative training failed over hundreds of trials, not reported in detail), and reversing to absolute rules cost about two weeks of performance; the value 'dichromat' is the authors' conclusion across all three paradigms and is not a count of cone classes

source.title: Dichromatic Colour Vision in Wallabies as Characterised by Three Behavioural Paradigms

quote: Our results consistently confirm the tammar wallaby as a dichromat.

value: calling males left their perches when an approaching UV-A light was 26.8 cm away (mean, +/-4.9 SE, N = 27)
method: field experiment: a handheld light (Streamlight Twin-Task 3C-UV) was moved slowly along a direct path toward a calling male from about 1.5 m, and the distance from perch to light when the frog left its perch was measured with a tape; each frog was tested in one of three conditions, light off, visible light or UV-A
conditions: wild adult males identified by calling, La Selva Biological Research Station, Costa Rica, 27 frogs in UV-A, 25 with the light off, 23 with visible light; the light condition was chosen at random for each frog; UV-A mode emitted 365 and 390 nm light at 0.30 uW/cm2 at 15 cm, visible mode 400 to 780 nm at 0.05 uW/cm2 at 15 cm, and the paper does not say whether the UV-A mode also emitted visible light, nor measure UV-A at the frogs' perches; approach speed is not given and the paper does not say observers were blind to condition; distance was recorded as 1 cm if the light came within 1 cm before the frog moved; mean departure distance was 16.7 cm (+/-3.1 SE) with the light off and 8.7 cm (+/-2.1 SE) with visible light (these two figures are from the page tool's summary of the next Results sentence, not quoted here); ANOVA F = 6.0, df 2 and 72, P < 0.01; Fisher's PLSD post-hoc UV-A versus visible P < 0.01, UV-A versus light off P = 0.05, visible versus off P = 0.14; frogs under visible light stayed longest and the authors say it is unclear why; a light approaching a frog is also an approaching object, and the response is not a measured spectral sensitivity; the number of non-responders is not reported separately
